 JUDGMENT This criminal appeal under Section 374 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 is filed assailing the judgment of conviction and order of sentence dated 27.7.2000 passed by learned Additional Sessions Judge Kukshi, District Dhar in S.T. No. 246 of 1999, whereby learned trial court convicted the appellants for offence punishable under Section 306 read with Section 34 of IPC and sentenced each of them for rigorous imprisonment for 3 years and fine of Rs. 500/- with default stipulation imprisonment for two months.

Appellant-Kalu son of Kesiya died during pendency of the appeal.
Therefore, appeal stands abated with reference to appellant-Kalu and his name was deleted from the cause title vide order dated 18.8.2001.
Present appeal is being prosecuted only with reference to appellant Nuru @ Noor Singh.

For sake of convenience,
appellant-Noor Singh shall be referred to as accused here-in-after.
3/ As per the case of prosecution, Richha Bai wife of accused-Nuru was found hanging by neck with the help of rope at her matrimonial home in the morning of 5.6.1999.
Police Station Bagh registered unnatural death intimation on information given by Kalu s/o Kesiya that his daughter-in-law has died due to hanging.
Sub Divisional Magistrate Kukshi conducted Panchanama of dead-body of Richha Bai and forwarded the dead-body for postmortem.
Medical officer, after postmortem examination, opined that Richcha Bai had died due to asphyxia caused by hanging within 24 hours of the postmortem examination.
During inquest proceedings, the statement of relatives of Richha Bai were recorded.
They alleged that Kalu, father-in-law of Richha Bai was harassing her for illicit-relations.
Kalu and his son Nuru were harassing her over petty domestic matters.
They were threatening to kill Richha Bai.
Richha Bai has committed suicide due to ill-treatment, man- handling, abuse and harassment of her husband Nuru and father-in-law Kalu.

On such allegations,
P.S. Bagh registered FIR at crime no. 92 of 1999 for offence punishable under Section 306 read with Section 34 of IPC against Nuru @ Noor Singh and Kalu.
The statement of witnesses were recorded.
On completion of investigation, final report was submitted before the learned Judicial Magistrate First Class Kukshi.
Learned Judicial Magistrate committed the case for trial to the Sessions Judge Dhar.

Learned Sessions Judge, Dhar framed charges for offence punishable under Section 306 and in the alternate, for the offence punishable under section 306 read with Section 34 of IPC against Kalu and Noor Singh.

On completion of trial, NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2024:MPHC-IND:31426 after hearing both the parties, learned Additional Sessions Judge, Kukshi, District Dhar convicted appellant Noor Singh for offence punishable under Section 306 read with Section 34 of IPC vide impugned judgment dated 27.7.2000 and sentenced him as stated in para 1 of this judgment.

sentences.text: On these ground, it is requested that appeal be allowed and impugned judgment dated 27.7.2000 be set aside while acquitting the accused.
6/ Learned counsel for appellant contended that there is no evidence with regard to cruelty by appellant-Noor Singh.
Main allegations were aimed at deceased Kalu.
Learned trial court committed in convicting the appellant on general and omnibus allegations of parents of deceased which were not corroborated by any evidence.
7/ Per-contra, learned counsel for State contended that deceased had committed suicide within three years of her marriage.
She was subjected to cruelty by her husband and father-in-law.
Therefore, in view of the NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2024:MPHC-IND:31426 presumption under Section 113A of Evidence Act, learned trial Court rightly convicted the appellant.
The appeal is meritless.
8/ Heard both the parties.
Perused the record.

9/ The points for determination in the present appeal are as under:-
i) Whether Richha Bai wife of Nuru committed suicide within three years of her marriage?
ii) Whether Richha Bai was subjected to cruelty as defined under Section 498-A of IPC by her husband and accused Nuru?
iii) Whether accused Nuru abetted suicide of Richha Bai?
POINTS FOR DETERMINATION No.1- REASONS FOR CONCLUSION 10/

Ramu Bai (PW-5)
mother of deceased Richha Bai, Misriya (PW-6), father of deceased Richha Bai and Kekadiya (PW-7)
cousin of deceased Richha Bai deposed that Richha Bai was married to Noor Singh three years before her death on the occasion of Akhatij.
This evidence is remained un- rebutted as the accused did not challenge factum of marriage with Richha Bai.
Village Choukidar Ter Singh (PW-3) stated that Kalu informed him that his daughter-in-law Richha Bai has died.
He went with Kalu to report the incident to P.S. Bagh.
The S.H.O. of P.S. Bagh D.S. Bilwad (PW-4) registered death intimation (Ex.P-5) as per the information given by Kalu.
The SDO(P) M.L.Jhari (PW-9) deposed that he conducted inquest into death of Richcha Bai.
He seized one Nylon rope vide seizure memo (Ex.P-10).
He conducted Panchanama of dead-body of Richha Bai (Ex.P-4) and forwarded the dead-body of Richcha Bai for postmortem examination vide application (Ex.P-1).
Dr. R.K. Shinde (PW-1) conducted postmortem examination of dead-body of Richha Bai on 6.6.1999 and gave detailed postmortem report (Ex.P-2).
The Medical officer opined that Richha Bai had died due to hanging within 24 hours of postmortem examination.
This evidence had remained unrebutted.
Therefore, learned trial Court has committed no error in concluding that Richha Bai had committed suicide within seven years of her marriage with accused Noor Singh.

Husband or relative of husband of a woman subjecting her to cruelty Whoever,
being the husband or the relative of the husband of a woman, subjects such woman to cruelty shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and shall also be liable to fine.
Explanation-

For the purpose of this section, "cruelty" means- (a) any willful conduct which is of such a nature as is likely to drive the woman to commit suicide or to cause grave injury or danger to life, limb or health (whether mental or physical) of the woman; or ;
.......................
11/ Prosecution had examined Ramu Bai (PW-5), mother of deceased Misriya (PW-6), father of deceased, Kekadiya (PW-7), cousin brother of deceased Dabu (PW-8) an acquaintance of the family.
Kekadiya (PW-7) and Dabu (PW-8) did not support the prosecution, rather, they supported the defence.
Ramu Bai (PW-5) and Misriya (PW-6) had made general and omnibus allegations against accused Nuru that Richha Bai used to tell that Nuru also misbehaves with her and occasionally beats her.
The allegations were directed mainly against Kalu.
Both the witness have stated that Kalu was harassing Richha Bai to have illicit relations with him.
Richha Bai was aggrieved by constant harassment of Kalu.
Kalu used to ill-treat her over household matters.
She was not permitted to visit her parental home.
But both of the witness did not tell any specific incident in proximity of death of Richha Bai.
Both of the witness have admitted that a few day before her death, Richha Bai had come to village Barkheda to attend marriage ceremony in house of Kekadiya.
Kekadiya (PW-7) stated that 2-3 days before her death, Richha Bai had come to village Barkheda and stayed for two days.
Thereafter, she returned to her matrimonial home at village Tol

None of the witness have stated that during her stay at village Barkheda, Richha Bai has made any complaint against the accused.
12/ Setara (DW-1) stated that Richha Bai had come to Barkheda to attend marriage at the house of Kekadiya.
In the marriage ceremony, Galiya caught hold of hand of Richha Bai.
There was a commotion.
Richha Bai returned with her husband.
Richha Bai had died due to embarrassment as Galiya had caught hold of her.
Bishan (PW-2) in cross-examination has admitted the suggestion that Galiya caught hold of Richha Bai at village Barkheda.
Richha Bai hanged herself due to embarrassment.

Ramubai (PW-5) although denied the suggestion, but Misriya (PW-6), father of deceased, admitted that he had heard that Galiya had caught hold of Richha Bai, when she was attending marriage at Barkheda.
On the same day, Richha Bai died at her matrimonial home.
These statement by the prosecution witness creates doubt on veracity of allegations of ill-treatment and cruelty alleged against the accused Nuru.
The prosecution evidence corroborates the defence evidence.
Thus probability of the defence is established.

Learned trial Court ignored these important aspects of the matter, therefore, the conclusion of the trial Court that Richha Bai was subjected to cruelty by the accused suffers from manifest impropriety.

sentences.text: Ramubai (PW-5) and Misriya (PW-6) have stated that there was a Panchayat in village Barkheda.
Kalu and Nuru had returned the articles of dowry in presence of Panch.
Ramubai was present at the time of Panchanama of dead-body of Richha Bai.
But no allegations were made at the time of Panchanama or Panchayat.
No complaint was ever lodged during lifetime of Richha Bai with regard to the harassment or ill-treatment by accused.

14/ Learned trial court in para 23 of the judgment cursorily rejected the defence evidence on conjecture and surmises that if any incident of NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2024:MPHC-IND:31426 molestation with Richha Bai had happened, it would have been reported or Galiya would have been socially outcasted by Panchayat.
Learned trial court completely ignored the inherent improbability and inconsistency of prosecution evidence as well as the corroboration of defence version by prosecution witness.
Thus, the learned trial court committed apparent error in concluding that prosecution has proved beyond doubt that Richha Bai was subjected to cruelty by accused Kalu and accused Nuru.
Accused Nuru aided accused Kalu in the act of cruelty.

POINT FOR DETERMINATION No.3- REASONS FOR CONCLUSION 15/ Section 113(A) of the Evidence Act provides as under :
113A:-

When the question is whether the commission of suicide by a woman had been abetted by her husband or any relative or her husband and it is shown that she had committed suicide within a period of seven years from the date of her marriage and that her husband or such relative of her husband had subjected her to cruelty, the court may presume, having regard to all the other circumstances of the case, that such suicide had been abetted by her husband or by such relative of her husband.
16/

Thus, where a woman commits suicide within seven years of marriage and it is shown that her husband had subjected her to cruelty as defined in section 498-A of IPC, the Court may presume, having regard to all the other circumstances of the case that such suicide had been abetted by her husband.
It is evident that the legislature was extremely careful in drafting this provision.

Had it been the intention of the legislature that the Court should in all cases raise the presumption that there has been abetment of suicide simply because suicide was committed by the woman within seven years of her marriage and she was subjected to cruelty, the legislature would not have used flexible expression as "the Court may presume, having regard to all the other circumstances of the case".
The expression may presume, postulates a discretionary presumption of fact.

The invocation NEUTRAL CITATION NO.
2024:MPHC-IND:31426 of the presumption must fulfill the proximity test to sustain conviction under section 306 of IPC on the charge of abetment to commit suicide, the cruelty or harassment must have been committed soon before her death. 17/
The Supreme Court in case of Rajbabu v. State of M.P., (2008) 17 SCC 526 observed as under- "20.

5 her husband, does not automatically give rise to the presumption that the suicide had been abetted by her husband or any relative of her husband.

sentences.text: The court is required to look into all the other circumstances of the case.

One of the circumstances which has to be considered by the court is whether the alleged cruelty was of such nature as was likely to drive the woman to commit suicide or to cause grave injury or danger to life,
limb or health of the woman.

The law has been succinctly stated in Ramesh Kumar v.
State of Chhattisgarh [(2001) 9 SCC 618 : 2002 SCC (Cri) 1088] wherein this Court observed: (SCC pp. 626-27, para 12) "12.

entities.text:
Ramesh Kumar v.
State of Chhattisgarh [(2001) 9 SCC 618 : 2002 SCC (Cri) 1088]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: This provision was introduced by the Criminal Law (Second) Amendment Act, 1983 with effect from 26-12-1983 to meet a social demand to resolve difficulty of proof where helpless married women were eliminated by being forced to commit suicide by the husband or in-laws and incriminating evidence was usually available within the four corners of the matrimonial home and hence was not available to anyone outside the occupants of the house.
However, still it cannot be lost sight of that the presumption is intended to operate against the accused in the field of criminal law.
Before the presumption may be raised, the foundation thereof must exist.

A bare reading of Section 113-A shows that to attract applicability of Section 113-A, it must be shown that (i) the woman has committed suicide, (ii) such suicide has been committed within a period of seven years from the date of her marriage, (iii) the husband or his relatives, who are charged had subjected her to cruelty.
On existence and availability of the abovesaid circumstances, the court may presume that such suicide had been abetted by her husband or by such relatives of her husband.
Parliament has chosen to NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2024:MPHC-IND:31426 sound a note of caution.
Firstly, the presumption is not mandatory; it is only permissive as the employment of expression 'may presume' suggests.

Secondly, the existence and availability of the abovesaid three circumstances shall not, like a formula, enable the presumption being drawn;
before the presumption may be drawn the court shall have to have regard to 'all the other circumstances of the case'.
A consideration of all the other circumstances of the case may strengthen the presumption or may dictate the conscience of the court to abstain from drawing the presumption.

The expression--'the other circumstances of the case' used in Section 113-A suggests the need to reach a cause-and-effect relationship between the cruelty and the suicide for the purpose of raising a presumption.
Last but not the least, the presumption is not an irrebuttable one.
In spite of a presumption having been raised the evidence adduced in defence or the facts and circumstances otherwise available on record may destroy the presumption.

The phrase 'may presume' used in Section 113-A is defined in Section 4 of the Evidence Act, which says--'Whenever it is provided by this Act that the court may presume a fact, it may either regard such fact as proved, unless and until it is disproved, or may call for proof of it.' "
18/ In the case of State of W.B. v. Orilal Jaiswal, (1994) 1 SCC 73, it was held that- 15.

entities.text: State of W.B. v. Orilal Jaiswal, (1994) 1 SCC 73
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: We are not oblivious that in a criminal trial the degree of proof is stricter than what is required in a civil proceedings.

In a criminal trial however intriguing may be facts and circumstances of the Nooru @ Noorsingh vs The State Of M.P. on 5 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/58438721/
6 case, the charges made against the accused must be proved beyond all reasonable doubts and the requirement of proof cannot lie in the realm of surmises and conjectures.

entities.text: Nooru @ Noorsingh vs The State Of M.P.
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The requirement of proof beyond reasonable doubt does not stand altered even after the introduction of Section 498-A IPC and Section 113-A of Indian Evidence Act.

Although, the court's conscience must be satisfied that the accused is not held guilty when there are reasonable doubts about the complicity of the accused in respect of the offences alleged, it should be borne in mind that there is no absolute standard for proof in a criminal trial NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2024:MPHC-IND:31426 and the question whether the charges made against the accused have been proved beyond all reasonable doubts must depend upon the facts and circumstances of the case and the quality of the evidences adduced in the case and the materials placed on record.

Lord Denning in Bater v. Bater [(1950) 2 All ER 458, 459 :
66 TLR (Pt. 2) 589] has observed that the doubt must be of a reasonable man and the standard adopted must be a standard adopted by a reasonable and just man for coming to a conclusion considering the particular subject-matter.

19/ The observations of the Supreme Court in a recent case of Naresh Kumar v. State of Haryana,
(2024) 3 SCC 573 are extracted as under- 23.

entities.text:
Naresh Kumar v. State of Haryana,
(2024) 3 SCC 573

sentences.text: Had there been any clinching evidence of incessant harassment on account of which the wife was left with no other option but to put an end to her life, it could have been said that the accused intended the consequences of his act, namely, suicide.

A person intends a consequence when he :
(1) foresees that it will happen if the given series of acts or omissions continue, and (2) desires it to happen.

The most serious level of culpability, justifying the most serious levels of punishment, is achieved when both these components are actually present in the accused's mind (a "subjective" test).
25.
It is now well settled that in order to convict a person under Section 306 IPC, there has to be a clear mens rea to commit the offence.
Mere harassment is not sufficient to hold an accused guilty of abetting the commission of suicide.
It also requires an active act or direct act which led the deceased to commit suicide.
The ingredient of mens rea cannot be assumed to be ostensibly present but has to be visible and conspicuous.
26. We take notice of the fact that the High Court has laid much emphasis on Section 113-A of the Evidence Act.
31. In this appeal, we are concerned with Section 113-A of the Evidence Act.
The mere fact that the deceased committed suicide within a period of seven years of her marriage, the presumption under Section 113-A of the Evidence Act would not automatically apply.

The legislative mandate is that where a woman commits suicide within seven years of her marriage and it is shown that her husband or any relative of her husband had subjected her to cruelty, the presumption NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2024:MPHC-IND:31426 under Section 113-A of the Evidence Act may be raised,
having regard to all other circumstances of the case, that such suicide had been abetted by her husband or by such relative of her husband.

7 32.

What is important to note is that the term "the court may presume having regard to all other circumstances of the case that such suicide had been abetted by her husband" would indicate that the presumption is discretionary, unlike the presumption under Section 113-B of the Evidence Act,
which is mandatory.
Therefore, before the presumption under Section 113-A is raised, the prosecution must show evidence of cruelty or incessant harassment in that regard.
33. The court should be extremely careful in assessing evidence under Section 113-A for finding out if cruelty was meted out.

If it transpires that a victim committing suicide was hypersensitive to ordinary petulance, discord and differences in domestic life quite common to the society to which the victim belonged and such petulance, discord and differences were not expected to induce a similarly circumstanced individual in a given society to commit suicide, the conscience of the court would not be satisfied for holding that the accused charged of abetting the offence of suicide was guilty.
35. This Court has held that from the mere fact of suicide within seven years of marriage, one should not jump to the conclusion of abetment unless cruelty was proved.
The court has the discretion to raise or not to raise the presumption, because of the words "may presume".
It must take into account all the circumstances of the case which is an additional safeguard.

36. In the absence of any cogent evidence of harassment or cruelty, an accused cannot be held guilty for the offence under Section 306IPC by raising presumption under Section 113-A.
37.
Before we part with this matter, we may only observe that the criminal justice system of ours can itself be a punishment.
It is exactly what has happened in this case.

It did not take more than 10 minutes for this Court to reach to an inevitable conclusion that the conviction of the appellant convict for the offence punishable under Section 306IPC is not sustainable in law.
The ordeal for the appellant started NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2024:MPHC-IND:31426 sometime in 1993 and is coming to the end in 2024 i.e. almost after a period of 30 years of suffering.
At the same time, we are also mindful of the fact that a young woman died leaving behind her 6-month-old infant.
No crime should go unpunished.
But at the same time, the guilt of the accused has to be determined in accordance with law.
To put it in other words, the guilt of the accused has to be determined on the basis of legal evidence on record.

39. In the case of accusation for abetment of suicide, the court should look for cogent and convincing proof of the act of incitement to the commission of suicide and such an offending action should be proximate to the time of occurrence.
Appreciation of evidence in criminal matters is a tough task and when it comes to appreciating the evidence in cases of abetment of suicide punishable under Section 306IPC, it is more arduous.
The court must remain very careful and vigilant in applying the correct principles of law governing the subject of abetment of suicide while appreciating the evidence on record.
Otherwise it may give an impression that the conviction is not legal but rather moral.
20/ The factual scenario revealed by the evidence on record is examined in the light of the afore-stated preposition of law.

The prosecution had failed to prove beyond doubt that Richha Bai Nooru @ Noorsingh vs The State Of M.P. on 5 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/58438721/
8 was subjected to cruelty by the accused Nuru in proximity of her death.

sentences.text: Learned trial court committed manifest error in raising the presumption under Section 113A of Evidence Act in the circumstances as revealed by the evidence on record.
There is no evidence that accused ever intended death of his wife Richha Bai.
The prosecution had failed to prove the mens-rea on part of accused for suicide of his wife.
Thus, the trial court had committed error in convicting the accused Nuru @ Noor Singh for offence punishable under Section 306 of IPC.

21/ Consequently, the appeal is allowed and impugned judgment of conviction and order of sentence dated 27.7.2000 passed in S.T. No. 246 of 1999 by learned Additional Sessions Judge, Kukshi,
District Dhar is set NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2024:MPHC-IND:31426 aside.
The accused/appellant Nuru @ Noor Singh is acquitted from charge of offence under Section 306 read with Section 34 of IPC.
His personal bond and surety bond for appearance stand discharged.
He shall be set at liberty forthwith.
The accused/appellant shall be entitled for remittance of fine amount, if deposited.
The order of trial court with regard to disposal of property is affirmed.
22/ Let record of the trial court along with a copy of this judgment be returned to concerned trial court for information and necessary compliance.
C.C. as per rules.
(SANJEEV S KALGAONKAR)

On existence and availability of the abovesaid circumstances, the court may presume that such suicide had been abetted by her husband or by such relatives of her husband.
A consideration of all the other circumstances of the case may strengthen the presumption or may dictate the conscience of the court to abstain from drawing the presumption.
The requirement of proof beyond reasonable doubt does not stand altered even after the introduction of Section 498-A IPC and Section 113-A of Indian Evidence Act.
Although, the court's conscience must be satisfied that the accused is not held guilty when there are reasonable doubts about the complicity of the accused in respect of the offences alleged, it should be borne in mind that there is no absolute standard for proof in a criminal trial NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2024:MPHC-IND:31426 and the question whether the charges made against the accused have been proved beyond all reasonable doubts must depend upon the facts and circumstances of the case and the quality of the evidences adduced in the case and the materials placed on record.
It is now well settled that in order to convict a person under Section 306 IPC, there has to be a clear mens rea to commit the offence.
Mere harassment is not sufficient to hold an accused guilty of abetting the commission of suicide.
It also requires an active act or direct act which led the deceased to commit suicide.
The ingredient of mens rea cannot be assumed to be ostensibly present but has to be visible and conspicuous.
The legislative mandate is that where a woman commits suicide within seven years of her marriage and it is shown that her husband or any relative of her husband had subjected her to cruelty, the presumption NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2024:MPHC-IND:31426 under Section 113-A of the Evidence Act may be raised,
having regard to all other circumstances of the case, that such suicide had been abetted by her husband or by such relative of her husband.
At the same time, we are also mindful of the fact that a young woman died leaving behind her 6-month-old infant.
No crime should go unpunished.
But at the same time, the guilt of the accused has to be determined in accordance with law.
To put it in other words, the guilt of the accused has to be determined on the basis of legal evidence on record.
39. In the case of accusation for abetment of suicide, the court should look for cogent and convincing proof of the act of incitement to the commission of suicide and such an offending action should be proximate to the time of occurrence.
Appreciation of evidence in criminal matters is a tough task and when it comes to appreciating the evidence in cases of abetment of suicide punishable under Section 306IPC, it is more arduous.
The court must remain very careful and vigilant in applying the correct principles of law governing the subject of abetment of suicide while appreciating the evidence on record.
Learned trial court committed manifest error in raising the presumption under Section 113A of Evidence Act in the circumstances as revealed by the evidence on record.
There is no evidence that accused ever intended death of his wife Richha Bai.
The prosecution had failed to prove the mens-rea on part of accused for suicide of his wife.
Thus, the trial court had committed error in convicting the accused Nuru @ Noor Singh for offence punishable under Section 306 of IPC.

District Dhar is set NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2024:MPHC-IND:31426 aside.
The accused/appellant Nuru @ Noor Singh is acquitted from charge of offence under Section 306 read with Section 34 of IPC.
